claims.text: A machine-learning model incorporating defect-induced scattering and oxygen impurity effects will improve electrical-conductivity prediction accuracy for bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model will outperform traditional analytical models based on perfect crystals over nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The material includes bulk HfNbTaTiZr variants with approximately 0 wt.% and 1 wt.% oxygen.
Atomistic simulations or physics-based descriptors of defect populations and oxygen distributions can be integrated with machine learning to predict conductivity.
Quantum and phonon scattering effects are significant in HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K.
Defect- and impurity-induced scattering dominate in HfNbTaTiZr over 300–1200 K.
The density and spatial distribution of dislocations, vacancies, and oxygen clusters mediate electron scattering.
Defects and oxygen impurities introduce non-ideal electron-scattering contributions absent from perfect-lattice analytical models.
Training on specimens with and without 1 wt.% oxygen will calibrate the effects of structural mediators on electron mobility and conductivity.
Capturing defect and impurity scattering will reduce prediction error relative to conventional analytical models.
The 1 wt.% oxygen sample will have lower conductivity because of increased electron scattering.
For near-ideal specimens, the model predictions will approach defect-free analytical predictions.
Perfect-crystal analytical approaches typically deviate significantly from measurements on non-ideal materials, especially materials containing oxygen impurities.
The proposed model is applicable from near 0 K to 1200 K and from nearly defect-free material to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Prediction accuracy outside 0–1200 K or at oxygen concentrations substantially beyond 1 wt.% is uncertain.
Sparse or poor-quality training data, low-temperature quantum effects, and high-temperature defect dynamics may limit prediction improvements.
Failure to reduce error by approximately 10–20% relative to analytical models, or deviations greater than ±20% from measurements, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial state describes the low-defect specimen only as being as close as possible to defect-free, whereas the experimental design calls it defect-free outright.
